items.title: Nvidia guarantees up to $105B in credit + invests $1.5B in SoftBank-backed SB Energy for OpenAI's PORTS-Pike Ohio data center (Aug 17) — first specific deal executed under the Aug 10 Nvidia $500B financing MOU framework; SB Energy builds/owns/operates 8 IT-GW campus under 20-year lease to OpenAI (initial 4.25 GW live-in-phases from 2028 with option for another 3.75 GW); Nvidia's SEC 8-K disclosed the site could take ~1.5 million Nvidia GPUs, translating to ~$150B–$200B in per-generation Nvidia revenue through 2030; paired: SB Energy + SoftBank commit $33.3B for 9.2 GW new natural-gas generation and $4.2B for regional grid infra via AEP Ohio partnership; site is former Cold-War Portsmouth uranium enrichment facility in Pike County; ~35,000 construction jobs through 2032, ~2,500 long-term operating jobs; scaled-back from the $250B backstop CNBC first reported July 27
items.summary: Nvidia disclosed on August 17 that it will provide up to $105 billion in credit guarantees to help build OpenAI's PORTS-Pike Technology Campus data center near Cincinnati, Ohio, and will separately invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy — the SoftBank-backed developer that will build, own, and operate the site under a 20-year lease to OpenAI (Nvidia Newsroom, Bloomberg, CNBC, Reuters, TechCrunch, Axios, Nikkei Asia, Crain's Cleveland Business, Investing.com, StockTitan, plus Nvidia's own Form 8-K filed with the SEC). The site will host 8 IT-gigawatts of AI compute capacity total: an initial 4.25 IT-GW built out in phases beginning 2028 (800 MW live 2028), with an option for an additional 3.75 IT-GW. Nvidia will be the exclusive compute supplier — every rack at PORTS-Pike will be Nvidia AI compute. New per Nvidia's Aug 17 SEC 8-K (per Yahoo Finance / Washington Examiner Aug 17–18 coverage): the full 8 IT-GW site could ultimately house on the order of 1.5 million Nvidia GPUs, corresponding to roughly $150 billion to $200 billion in potential Nvidia revenue per chip generation deployed at the site through 2030 — a specific per-generation figure that grounds why the $105B credit-guarantee tranche is bankable against Nvidia's own downstream sell-through. Powering the 8 IT-GW of compute: SB Energy and SoftBank plan to build at least 10 GW of new energy generation (per SB Energy's separate $33.3 billion Japanese-funded natural-gas generation build-out — 9.2 GW of new natural-gas capacity at the site), plus $4.2 billion in regional grid infrastructure investment through a partnership with AEP Ohio. Location context: the campus sits on private land plus federal property formerly used for uranium enrichment during the Cold War (the Portsmouth Site in Pike County ceased enrichment operations in 2001). Jobs impact: ~35,000 construction jobs through 2032 plus ~2,500 long-term operating jobs. Financial framing per Reuters/Bloomberg/CNBC: this is the largest arrangement of its type Nvidia has ever entered, and it represents a substantial scale-back from the $250 billion backstop CNBC first reported on July 27 was under discussion (Nvidia had reportedly been in talks to guarantee up to $250B and to separately finance up to $350B in chips for the site). The refined $105B guarantee is what the debt markets and Nvidia's balance sheet actually accommodated. This deal is also the first specific transaction executed under the framework of the Aug 10 Nvidia $500B AI-infrastructure-financing MOU with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR (covered as its own item in yesterday's am file) — the treat-GPU-compute-as-project-finance-collateral model was designed exactly to make deals like this bankable. What has NOT been disclosed: the specific tranche structure of the $105B credit line, which of the six MOU banks will underwrite what portion, the exact per-token or per-GPU-hour economics OpenAI will pay under the 20-year lease, whether OpenAI's committed take-or-pay covers all 8 IT-GW or only the initial 4.25 GW, whether the option-tranche exercise is at Nvidia's or SB Energy's discretion, and the specific chip generation (Blackwell / Rubin / next-gen) targeted for the 2028 first-phase live date.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: this is the specific first concrete transaction under the Aug 10 Nvidia $500B AI-infrastructure-financing MOU that sits as its own item in yesterday's morning section. Four things to note. First, the specific scale of what's being committed: 8 IT-gigawatts is roughly 2× the total electrical consumption of the entire U.S. cryptocurrency mining industry in 2024, or about 5% of Ohio's peak state-wide grid load, dedicated to a single tenant (OpenAI) on a single site under a single 20-year lease. The specific initial-phase live date of 2028 for the first 800 MW is real construction — data-center-scale grid interconnects take 24–36 months from executed lease to live capacity even when everything goes right, and Ohio's PJM interconnect queue is one of the most congested in the U.S. right now. That's the specific tell that the deal was structured with realistic timelines rather than marketing-announcement timelines. Second, the SEC-8-K disclosure that surfaced overnight — that the full site could house ~1.5 million Nvidia GPUs, corresponding to roughly $150B–$200B in Nvidia revenue per chip generation deployed through 2030 — is the specific piece of new information that reframes the $105B credit-guarantee number as economically bounded rather than a naked exposure. Nvidia is effectively guaranteeing $105B against $150B–$200B of near-certain sell-through per generation to the same physical site; at ~2–3 chip-generation refresh cycles between 2028 and 2035, the underlying downstream revenue is comfortably multiple hundreds of billions. That's the specific accounting-and-market read for why the guarantee actually cleared debt-market underwriting even at $105B: it isn't a subsidy, it's advance financing against captive future revenue Nvidia already knows it will book. Third, the specific $105B-vs-$250B scale-back is the interesting piece of financial-market context. CNBC first reported July 27 that Nvidia was in talks to guarantee up to $250B for the site, and Tom's Hardware had reporting on a possible $350B chip-financing tranche on top of that. The refined $105B guarantee announced Aug 17 is what actually cleared debt-market underwriting — that's the specific signal that even at $105B, this is a bigger project-finance commitment than any single infrastructure vendor has ever made for one tenant. The read for anyone modeling AI-industry economics: the market is willing to underwrite the biggest guarantee in project-finance history for OpenAI compute, but not the ~2× larger one Nvidia originally proposed. That's a specific data point about where the marginal appetite sits. Fourth, this deal is the specific concrete example that the Aug 10 $500B MOU framework (in yesterday's am file) is not aspirational — it's already executing. The specific practical read for Gabe as a Python developer: OpenAI now has a locked-in 8 IT-GW compute floor starting 2028, which means the pricing floor at the OpenAI API is going to keep trending down through 2028–2032 as this capacity comes online, and OpenAI now has the specific compute headroom to keep undercutting Anthropic on model-tier pricing without running into supply constraints. That's the specific counter-signal to the Anthropic $2T IPO story in yesterday's am file: while Anthropic is locking in visible compute commitments ahead of a public offering, OpenAI is locking in even bigger ones ahead of its own confidential-filing-to-live-IPO process (OpenAI filed its own S-1 June 8). The specific power-generation detail worth internalizing: 9.2 GW of new natural-gas capacity being built at the site is the specific tell that renewables-only power did not clear the reliability bar for a facility that's supposed to run at ~90%+ utilization 24/7 for 20 years. That's a specific practical read on where AI-compute-power baseload is going: gas turbines, not solar+battery. Watch over the next 90 days: (1) which specific banks from the Aug 10 MOU consortium underwrite the $105B guarantee tranches; (2) whether the option-tranche 3.75 IT-GW gets exercised early; (3) whether the SB Energy natural-gas buildout triggers any specific Ohio EPA or federal permit challenges; (4) whether any specific counter-deal announcements land from Microsoft (for its own OpenAI-hosting capacity) or from AWS (for Anthropic-hosting capacity) in response to the visible scale of the Nvidia-SB Energy commitment.

items.title: Unitree unveils 'Superman' high-speed humanoid robot (Aug 17) days ahead of its Shanghai STAR-Market debut TOMORROW (Wed Aug 19) — first general-purpose robotics company to list on mainland China; company claims Superman was built in ~3 months, hits 12.66 m/s top speed (past Usain Bolt's 100m peak of 12.42 m/s) and clears a 2-metre standing jump — figures are self-reported and unverified by outside parties; the $9.04B IPO ($905M / 6.1B yuan raised at 150.8 yuan/share) was over 8,000× oversubscribed by retail on STAR — an all-time record; grey-market pricing as of Aug 18 (CNN Business, Caixin Global) points to a first-day gain of 3–4× the offer price; DeepSeek is among strategic investors
items.summary: China's Unitree Robotics unveiled a new high-speed humanoid robot on Monday August 17, dubbed 'Superman,' two days before becoming the first general-purpose robotics company to list on mainland China's stock market — trading opens tomorrow, Wednesday August 19 (Yahoo Finance/Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC, ChinaTechNews, Humanoids Daily, Recode China AI, Digitimes, Autonews Gasgoo, Cryptopolitan, Gizmodo, BusinessWorld, The Express Tribune, Startup Fortune). Unitree says Superman was developed in just over three months and posts benchmark specs that meaningfully exceed prior Unitree humanoids: a standing jump of 2 metres and a top running speed of 12.66 metres per second (~28.3 mph), which per Yahoo Finance's headline outpaces Usain Bolt's 100-metre peak of ~12.42 m/s — a first for a general-purpose humanoid platform per the coverage. Important overnight caveat surfacing in Aug 17–18 secondary reporting (Cryptopolitan, Gizmodo, Yahoo Finance follow-ups): the Superman speed and jump numbers are entirely self-reported by Unitree and have not been independently verified by any outside party — the outside record is a fast H1 demo, founder Wang Xingxing's bold public predictions, and a hot IPO, not an independently-clocked Superman outrunning Bolt. Reporters are explicit that the reveal appears timed in part to generate buzz for the IPO. The unveil landed as pre-IPO buzz, two days before Unitree's Shanghai STAR-Market debut. IPO structure: priced August 6 at 150.8 yuan per share ($22.34), raising 6.1 billion yuan (~$905 million) at a company valuation of approximately 61 billion yuan ($9.04 billion). The retail-tranche demand was record-breaking: Bloomberg reported Aug 10 that the Shanghai retail tranche was 5,526× oversubscribed and later reporting (Yahoo Finance/Reuters/Quartz Aug 17) put the peak-oversubscription figure at more than 8,000×, an all-time record for the STAR Market. New as of Aug 18 (CNN Business, Caixin Global, The Next Web, Domain-B): grey-market pricing is pointing to first-day gains of 3–4× the offer price of 150.8 yuan, implying a potential debut price in the 450–600 yuan range; Chinese new listings returned an average of 233% on debut in the first half of 2026, per KraneShares / Domain-B analysis, which sets the baseline for what 'exuberant' looks like on the STAR Market right now. Chinese AI company DeepSeek is disclosed as one of the strategic investors participating in the IPO cornerstone allocation. Company context: Unitree is the world's largest humanoid-robot maker by sales and has cumulatively produced roughly 18,000 bipedal humanoids to date (per Aug 3 Digitimes reporting on 1H26 revenue up 35%+ on humanoid demand). Trading is expected to open on the Shanghai Stock Exchange on Wednesday August 19. What has NOT been publicly disclosed: independent third-party verification of the Superman speed/jump numbers, Superman's price point, the specific customer segments Superman is targeted at, the manufacturing capacity ramp target for Superman for 2027, and whether the Superman platform is available for pre-order or is currently a demonstrator-only unit.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: this is worth internalizing as the specific concrete data point that grounds where the humanoid-robotics market is actually heading, and it pairs with two things worth watching outside your HTML/CSS/Python day-to-day. Also worth noting: trading opens TOMORROW (Wed Aug 19), so this is the last morning brief before the debut and the demand-vs-first-day-price data point lands. Four things to note. First, the specific speed and jump numbers are the interesting technical signal — with an important caveat that surfaced overnight. 12.66 m/s top speed exceeds Usain Bolt's 100-metre peak of ~12.42 m/s, and 2-metre standing jumps put Superman ahead of every Boston Dynamics Atlas demo Unitree has been benchmarked against. But these numbers are entirely self-reported by Unitree and have not been independently verified by any outside party — Cryptopolitan, Gizmodo, and the Yahoo Finance follow-up all flag this explicitly. What's specifically hard about achieving those numbers on a bipedal humanoid isn't the raw actuator power — it's the real-time balance and joint-force control at velocities where fall recovery has ~100ms of window. If the numbers hold under independent test, Unitree developing that capability in ~3 months from concept to demo is the pace signal that matters: Chinese humanoid capability is on an actively-shrinking-development-cycle-time curve, not a linear-improvement curve. If they don't hold, this reads as an IPO-timed marketing spec — worth being calibrated on either outcome rather than accepting the numbers at face value. The specific practical read for anyone thinking about robotics: the gap between 'Chinese humanoids are cheaper but less capable' and 'Chinese humanoids match or exceed Western humanoids' has largely closed on locomotion benchmarks over the last 12 months, and Superman would be the specific data point that closes it — pending verification. Second, the IPO details tell you something specific about Chinese capital markets. 8,000× oversubscription is an all-time STAR Market record — the previous record was ~4,000× and it stood for years. New from this morning (Aug 18): grey-market pricing is pointing to a first-day gain of 3–4× the 150.8-yuan offer price, and Chinese new listings returned an average of 233% on debut in H1 2026 — so a dramatic pop is the baseline, not a surprise. The specific practical read is that Chinese retail is treating humanoid-robotics IPOs as the next-generation equivalent of the electric-vehicle IPOs of 2020-2022, and the DeepSeek cornerstone allocation is the specific tell that the leading Chinese AI companies are positioning humanoid embodiment as a core part of their forward roadmap. Third, the specific relevance to what you write in Python: humanoid-robotics platforms will increasingly ship with Python-first SDKs for research and application development. Unitree's existing G1 SDK is Python-first, and Superman's SDK will very likely follow the same pattern. If you're curious about robotics as an adjacent domain worth broadening into, Unitree's post-IPO documentation push is the specific artifact worth watching in the next 60 days. Fourth, on the IPO-buzz-vs-real-capability read: the timing of the Superman unveil (two trading days before debut) plus the self-reported-and-unverified caveat is the specific reason to keep the announcement in the 'signalling' bucket rather than the 'confirmed capability' bucket until an independent test surfaces. Watch over the next 30 days: (1) whether any independent third-party reproduces or challenges the 12.66 m/s and 2m-jump figures; (2) how the grey-market pricing compares to the actual Aug 19 first-day open; (3) Superman's pricing and pre-order availability once Unitree drops product-page details; (4) whether the DeepSeek cornerstone allocation translates into a specific product-integration announcement; (5) whether any specific Western humanoid company publishes updated benchmark numbers in response to the Superman spec.

items.title: Higgsfield closes $400M Series B at $5.4B valuation (Aug 17) — 4× step-up from the $1.3B Series A in just 8 months; annualized revenue $700M this month vs $20M a year ago (35× YoY); 30M users across 238 countries; powers visual production for 390 of the Fortune 500; agentic-product users up 42× in three months since the Supercomputer rollout in May, now driving 20M+ content generations/month; DST Global-led with Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Intel Capital, Tribe Capital, Smash Capital, Fifth Wall, Valor Capital, Liberty Global Tech Ventures, Mirae Asset Capital, NTT DOCOMO Ventures
items.summary: Higgsfield — the AI video and image generation platform aimed at professional creators, brands, agencies, and studios — announced on August 17 a $400 million Series B financing at a $5.4 billion valuation (Higgsfield/PRNewswire, Yahoo Finance, TechCrunch, SiliconANGLE, Pulse2, BNN Bloomberg, Quartz, BigGo Finance, Ascendants, Financial Times/Seeking Alpha). The Series B was led by DST Global with participation from Tribe Capital, Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Smash Capital, Fifth Wall, Valor Capital, Intel Capital, Liberty Global Tech Ventures, Mirae Asset Capital, NTT DOCOMO Ventures, plus existing investors including Accel, Menlo Ventures, AI Capital Partners, GFT Ventures, Capra Ventures, BAM Corner Point, and BroadLight Capital. The valuation represents roughly a 4× step-up from Higgsfield's previously disclosed $1.3 billion Series A — a jump that landed in just 8 months per TechCrunch's Aug 17 reporting. Business-metrics context per Higgsfield's own announcement and TechCrunch follow-up: annualized revenue reached $700 million this month, up from $20 million a year earlier (a 35× year-over-year growth rate); the platform serves more than 30 million users globally across 238 countries and territories, with the United States as the largest single market; Higgsfield now powers visual production for 390 of the Fortune 500 — a specific enterprise-penetration figure surfaced in overnight coverage that grounds the professional-tier positioning; agentic-AI users grew 42-fold in three months following the company's Supercomputer product rollout in May 2026, and the agentic tools are now responsible for more than 20 million content generations per month. Use of proceeds per the company: R&D, global infrastructure, AI talent recruitment, and international go-to-market expansion. Strategic context: Higgsfield's Aug 17 raise is the largest AI-video-focused financing round disclosed in 2026 by more than 2× (per SiliconANGLE), and the round lands as Runway and Pika (Higgsfield's two closest Western competitors on the professional-creator side) are both reportedly in-market with their own capital raises but at earlier-stage valuations. The Financial Times' framing (via Seeking Alpha follow-up): 'Is AI video back?' — the round is being read across financial press as the specific data point that resolves whether the mid-2025 AI-video-startup pullback was permanent or transitory, with the answer clearly being 'transitory' at professional-creator scale. What has NOT been disclosed: Higgsfield's gross margin structure, the specific compute cost per content generation, specific named enterprise customers within the Fortune-500-390 figure, whether NTT DOCOMO Ventures' participation implies a specific Japanese-market distribution partnership, and the specific timeline for any Higgsfield IPO.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: this is worth internalizing as the specific data point that anchors where the professional-tier AI-video market is heading and where the money is actually flowing. Four things to note. First, the specific $700M-annualized-revenue-vs-$20M-a-year-ago figure is the interesting piece of unit-economics context, and it's specifically not the same story as the free-tier consumer AI-video race (Sora, Veo, Kling, Runway Gen-4). Higgsfield's positioning is 'professional creators, brands, agencies, studios' — the customer segment that pays four-figure monthly subscriptions rather than $10-$30 consumer tiers. 35× revenue growth in a year at that positioning is the specific tell that the professional-video segment has crossed a specific quality-and-workflow-integration threshold in the last 6-9 months. That threshold is what the Supercomputer product (rolled out May 2026) unlocked — the 42× three-month growth in agentic-product users is the specific concrete measurement of what happens when a professional-tier AI-video platform ships genuinely autonomous multi-scene generation with production-quality output. Second, the new specific data point surfaced overnight — Higgsfield powers visual production for 390 of the Fortune 500 — is the specific enterprise-penetration figure that turns the $700M-annualized number from 'high-growth story' into 'entrenched-supplier-in-the-Fortune-500-marketing-stack' story. 390-of-500 penetration is the specific tell that Higgsfield is not competing with Runway/Pika for a shrinking pool of top-tier logos — it's already inside most of them. That specifically explains why DST Global was willing to lead at a 4×-in-8-months step-up: the recurring-revenue moat inside the Fortune 500 is durable in a way that consumer AI-video subscriptions are not. Third, the specific investor lineup is worth reading closely as a signal. DST Global as lead is the specific tell that this is being underwritten as a growth-stage-Uber-scale investment rather than an early-tech-venture bet — DST typically enters at scale-transition inflection points, not at product-fit-discovery moments. items.title: Microsoft begins rolling out the unified Copilot app today (Aug 18) — Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot merge into one app with a new icon and new URL (copilot.cloud.microsoft); web and mobile go live worldwide now, Windows/Mac desktop in early preview today with broad rollout mid-September; work and personal accounts stay separate by design
items.summary: Microsoft began the worldwide rollout of its unified Copilot app on August 18, merging its consumer Microsoft Copilot product and the enterprise Microsoft 365 Copilot app into a single application that handles both personal (Microsoft Account) and work (Microsoft Entra ID) accounts (Windows Central, Unite.AI, support.microsoft.com, m365admin.handsontek.net, Petri, ElevenForum, FutureWork Blog). The app ships today with a new unified icon — replacing the distinct consumer and enterprise Copilot icons — and the browser URL moves from m365.cloud.microsoft to copilot.cloud.microsoft, with automatic redirects in place for users on the old URL. The mobile app rollout (iOS and Android) is worldwide beginning August 18; the Windows and Mac desktop app is in early preview today, with broad deployment scheduled for mid-September. Work accounts (Microsoft Entra/Microsoft 365) and personal accounts (Microsoft Account) remain separate by design — data does not flow between them — but users who have both can access each from within the same app. The app keeps the 'Microsoft Copilot' name, dropping the 'Microsoft 365 Copilot' branding for the enterprise experience as a separate product. Microsoft announced the merger and detailed its technical plan on August 14; today is the go-live date for the web and mobile tiers. The Partner Center change log (Microsoft Learn) confirms August 18 as the official rollout start for account-separation UX and URL transition.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: if you use anything in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem — Outlook, OneDrive, Teams, even just a Microsoft account for Xbox or Bing — the Copilot experience is changing today, and there are a few things worth tracking as a developer. First, the UX architecture: Microsoft is betting on a single AI interface for work and personal rather than two separate apps, and the 'data does not flow between accounts' guardrail is the specific design signal that enterprise security teams in regulated industries (finance, healthcare, government) need to hear before deploying Copilot broadly. The fact that Microsoft explicitly leads with the data-separation guarantee suggests this has been the single biggest adoption blocker in enterprise rollouts — not capability, but the fear that personal-account AI interactions might bleed into managed-device work data. Second, the URL change (m365.cloud.microsoft → copilot.cloud.microsoft) is the specific telltale that Microsoft is rebranding this as an AI-first product rather than a Microsoft 365 productivity add-on — the brand hierarchy is now 'Copilot' at the top with M365 as the underlying capability set. That's a meaningful signal about where Microsoft's AI-product roadmap is headed: Copilot becomes the front door to the entire Microsoft app graph, not a chat box stapled to Word. Third, the practical Python-developer angle: if you've ever scripted against the Microsoft Graph API (the REST API that powers Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, and everything else M365), the underlying API is unchanged — this is a UX-layer unification, not an API break. But the new desktop app (early preview today) is the specific artifact to watch for agentic-automation integrations, since Copilot's desktop presence is where Microsoft is building cross-app agent workflows that can act across Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Teams with minimal friction. That's the specific path from 'Python script that calls the Graph API' to 'agent that can compose, read, and act on M365 documents autonomously' — and the unified app is the visible shell of that infrastructure.
